questions.sub_skill: Configure and deploy AI Gateway in Azure API Management for Microsoft Foundry
questions.prompt: One application's runaway loop starves every other consumer of your Foundry deployment. Token metrics show a single consumer at its limit. What is most likely misconfigured?
options: The token limit is set per minute rather than per day
The llm-token-limit counter key is a constant rather than the subscription, so all consumers share one counter
Semantic caching is disabled
The backend pool has no circuit breaker
questions.explanation: Limiting by a key every consumer shares reproduces the problem you were solving. A per-consumer counter key — the subscription ID — means one application hitting its limit leaves the others working.
why_not: The window size changes how quickly a consumer reaches its limit, not whether one consumer's usage starves the others.
Semantic caching reduces backend calls for repeated prompts. It does not separate one consumer's quota from another's.
A circuit breaker protects against a failing backend. The problem here is one shared token counter.

questions.sub_skill: Configure and deploy AI Gateway in Azure API Management for Microsoft Foundry
questions.prompt: A requirement says oversized prompts must be rejected before they reach the model, so no backend cost is incurred. Which setting?
options: Semantic caching with a low similarity threshold
estimate-prompt-tokens on the llm-token-limit policy
A backend circuit breaker
An llm-emit-token-metric dimension on prompt length
questions.explanation: The token limit policy can precalculate prompt tokens at the gateway, so a request that already exceeds the limit never reaches the backend at all.
why_not: Semantic caching answers repeated prompts from the cache. It does not reject oversized ones.
A circuit breaker reacts to backend failures. It does not measure prompt size.
Emitting a metric reports token usage after the fact. It rejects nothing.

questions.sub_skill: Enable Defender for AI Service in Cloud Workload Protection in Defender for Cloud
questions.prompt: Your team enables content filters on a Foundry deployment and considers indirect prompt injection handled. Why is it not?
options: Content filters apply only to completions, never to prompts
Content filters govern harm categories in content; detecting instructions hidden in retrieved material is what Prompt Shields does
Content filters are disabled whenever groundedness detection is enabled
Indirect injection can only be addressed at the API Management gateway
questions.explanation: Prompt Shields detects the attack — direct and indirect injection attempts. Content filters govern the content. An injection carried in a retrieved document is not a harm-category problem, and treating it as one is how organisations conclude they have handled something they have not.
why_not: The direction filters apply in is not the problem. An injection hidden in retrieved content is not a harm category, so content filters do not look for it.
Groundedness detection does not switch content filters off. The gap is that detecting injection is Prompt Shields' job.
Prompt Shields, in Foundry, is the control built to detect direct and indirect injection attempts. The gateway is not the only place to address it.

questions.sub_skill: Configure guardrails for agent security in Foundry
questions.prompt: Defender for Cloud raises a prompt injection alert on a Foundry workload. The SOC asks what the prompt said. Under what configuration can you answer?
options: Always — alerts include the full prompt by default
Only if the suspicious prompt evidence extension was enabled; otherwise the alert exists and the content does not
Only if Microsoft Purview is connected to the subscription
Only if the workload uses API Management with request logging
questions.explanation: Suspicious prompt evidence is an optional extension of the AI workloads plan, off by default. With it on, short redacted snippets of the triggering prompts surface in Defender XDR. Without it, the alert fires and the evidence was never captured.
why_not: Alerts do not include prompt content by default. Suspicious prompt evidence is an optional extension, off by default.
Connecting Purview is not what captures this evidence. It comes from the AI workloads plan's suspicious prompt evidence extension.
The alert's own evidence comes from the suspicious prompt evidence extension. Without it, the alert fires with no prompt content attached.

questions.sub_skill: Monitor AI security by using the Data and AI security dashboard in Defender for Cloud
questions.prompt: A Foundry project sits in a subscription where the AI workloads plan has never been enabled. What does Defender for Cloud know about it?
options: Everything — discovery is automatic once Defender for Cloud is enabled
Nothing; discovery of AI services is a consequence of enabling the plan, so the workload does not appear in the Data and AI security dashboard
Its configuration but not its runtime behaviour
Only its attack paths, from the cloud security graph
questions.explanation: Enabling the plan is what triggers discovery of Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI and Azure Machine Learning resources, with results appearing in the Data and AI security dashboard within minutes. Without it, the workload is entirely unmonitored.
why_not: Enabling Defender for Cloud alone does not discover AI services. Discovery is triggered by enabling the AI workloads plan.
Without the plan the workload is not discovered as an AI workload at all, so it does not appear in the Data and AI security dashboard.
The plan is what triggers discovery of AI services. Without it, Defender for Cloud has no AI-specific view of the workload.
